planting.note: Plant divisions or plantlets in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; piggyback plant readily propagates itself from the small plantlets that form at the base of mature leaves — simply pin a leaf to moist soil to root a new plant.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil in partial to full shade; keep consistently moist, since the shallow-rooted foliage wilts quickly in dry conditions. Tolmiea menziesii (piggyback plant, or youth-on-age) is a native Pacific Northwest woodland groundcover named for its unusual and endearing method of vegetative reproduction: new baby plantlets sprout directly at the base of each mature, hairy, maple-like leaf, riding piggyback on the parent leaf until the weight bends the stem to the ground, where the plantlet roots and becomes an independent plant. Small, unusual, chocolate-brown and green tubular flowers appear on slender stalks in spring, though the fresh green, textured foliage and self-propagating habit are the plant's main appeal. It forms a dense, low, weed-suppressing mat in consistently moist, shaded woodland conditions, and its easy self-propagation makes it simple to share and spread through a shade garden. Also grown widely as a houseplant, it performs equally well outdoors in the reliably moist, cool shade it needs, zone 6–9.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Japanese roof iris is unusual among irises for genuinely thriving in partial shade, and was historically planted directly into thatched roofs in Japan, where it tolerated thin soil and part-day sun.

directions: Plant shallow rhizome divisions, barely covered, in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most bearded and beardless irises, which demand full sun, Japanese roof iris flowers reliably in dappled shade, making it a rare shade-tolerant iris option. In late spring, the fans of broad, ribbed, glossy leaves send up flattened stems topped with large, flat-faced, lavender-blue flowers marked with a distinctive white and violet crested pattern on the falls, resembling a small Japanese iris (Iris ensata) in form though considerably more shade-adapted and drought-tolerant once established. Its historic use rooted directly into Japanese thatched roofs, where it survived on minimal soil and inconsistent moisture, speaks to its toughness and adaptability. An excellent, unusual choice for adding iris-type flowers to a partly shaded border or woodland-edge planting where full-sun irises would fail to bloom, zone 4–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; London Pride forms a dense, spreading evergreen rosette mat and tolerates deep shade and root competition from established trees better than most flowering groundcovers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; tolerates deep, dry shade under mature trees better than most flowering shade groundcovers once established. Saxifraga × urbium (London Pride) is a classic cottage-garden hybrid saxifrage forming neat, evergreen rosettes of small, spoon-shaped, leathery leaves that knit together into a dense, weed-suppressing mat. In late spring, airy, wiry stems rise well above the foliage carrying loose sprays of small, star-shaped, pale pink flowers speckled with deeper pink and red spots — a delicate, long-lasting display that contrasts nicely with the low, tidy foliage below. Long a staple of English shade gardens, it has largely fallen out of fashion in American gardening despite being one of the toughest, most reliable evergreen groundcovers for difficult dry shade, tolerating root competition, poor soil, and neglect better than most alternatives. An excellent, underused choice for edging a shaded path or filling in beneath established shrubs and trees, zone 6–8.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; candelabra primrose needs steady moisture and is best sited at a pond edge, streamside, or damp low spot rather than an average garden bed.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; never allow the soil to dry out. Primula bulleyana is a Chinese species of candelabra primrose, named for the distinctive way its flowers are arranged in tiered whorls stacked up the flower stalk like the branching arms of a candelabra — in late spring to early summer, the stems carry several tiers of bright orange to apricot-yellow flowers rising well above the coarse, crinkled basal foliage, an especially vivid color break from the pinks and purples of many other primroses. Like other candelabra-type primroses, it thrives at the damp margins of a pond, stream, or bog garden, where reliably moist, humus-rich soil lets it naturalize and self-seed into an increasingly showy colony over the years. A striking, colorful choice for the moist partial shade of a woodland bog garden or streamside planting, zone 5–8.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant pseudobulbs or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; unlike most terrestrial orchids, Bletilla species are genuinely easy to grow in an ordinary garden bed without special mycorrhizal requirements, spreading gradually by pseudobulb offsets into a larger clump.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; mulch in colder parts of its range to protect the shallow pseudobulbs over winter. Bletilla ochracea (yellow Chinese ground orchid) is a rare, genuinely garden-friendly terrestrial orchid from China, closely related to the more commonly available purple-flowered Bletilla striata but distinguished by its soft, buttery yellow blooms — an unusual flower color among hardy garden orchids. In late spring, slender stems rise from pleated, lance-shaped leaves carrying several elegant, orchid-shaped flowers that persist for weeks, followed by attractive seed pods if left unpicked. Unlike most native terrestrial orchids, which require a very specific symbiotic soil fungus and are essentially impossible to establish from purchased stock, Bletilla species grow readily in ordinary humus-rich garden soil and slowly multiply into an increasingly showy clump, making them one of the few hardy orchids genuinely suitable for typical home garden conditions. An excellent, unusual specimen for a partly shaded border, zone 6–9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
